explain.say: Batteries give DC, which flows steadily one way, while power stations send AC, which transformers can easily step up and down. Chargers turn AC into DC for your gadgets.

faq.a: Direct current, DC, flows in one direction only, from a battery's negative end round to its positive end. Batteries, solar cells and the output of phone chargers all give DC.
Alternating current, AC, keeps reversing direction. Mains electricity flips back and forth 50 times a second in the UK and Europe and 60 times a second in North America.

faq.q: Why do power stations make AC?
faq.a: Spinning generators naturally make AC, and AC can be stepped up and down easily with transformers, so it can travel long distances at high voltage with little waste.

faq.q: Why do phones need a charger to turn AC into DC?
faq.a: Electronics need a small, steady one-way current. The charger lowers the voltage and uses diodes and capacitors to turn the flipping AC into smooth DC.

faq.q: What was the war of the currents?
faq.a: In the late 1880s, Thomas Edison backed DC while George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla promoted AC. AC won for power grids because transformers made long-distance transmission practical.

facts: UK and European mains electricity alternates at 50 hertz; North America uses 60 hertz.
